nameStory: The Red-backed Orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive reddish-brown coloration on its rounded abdomen that looks like it's wearing a rusty backpack. This warm-toned 'back' contrasts beautifully with its bright green legs and front body section. The name perfectly captures what jumps out at you when you spot one of these colorful spiders in their classic round webs.
description: The Red-backed Orbweaver is a medium-sized spider that looks like nature's artist got creative with a paintbrush. Its most striking feature is the contrast between its bright green legs and front body (called the cephalothorax) and its reddish-brown rounded abdomen decorated with white markings. Like other orbweavers, it spins the classic circular webs we all recognize, with neat radiating spokes and spiral threads. These spiders are part of a large family of web-building specialists that help control flying insect populations.

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Look for the signature two-tone coloring: bright green legs and front body section contrasting with a reddish-brown, rounded abdomen marked with white spots or patches

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic circular orb webs with radiating spokes and spiral capture threads that feel sticky to the touch if you accidentally walk into one

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The abdomen is distinctly rounded and plump, especially in females, giving it an almost globe-like appearance when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: White markings on the reddish-brown abdomen create patterns that may remind you of abstract art or inkblots against the warm background color

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized for an orbweaver, with females noticeably larger and more robust than the smaller, more slender males

habitat: Red-backed Orbweavers prefer wooded areas and forest edges throughout New England, where they can anchor their webs between trees, shrubs, and tall vegetation. They're often found in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests, particularly where there are clearings or gaps that provide good flying insect traffic. Look for them in areas with adequate moisture and protection from strong winds.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging and become active as temperatures warm, starting to build their characteristic orb webs in promising locations between vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible in their webs, actively hunting flying insects and mating. This is the best time to spot their distinctive green and reddish-brown coloration.
seasonality.fall: Females may be carrying egg sacs or laying eggs before the first hard frosts. Webs may become less maintained as the season progresses and spiders prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off with hard frosts, though eggs overwinter in protected locations to emerge as spiderlings the following spring.

funFact: Red-backed Orbweavers are like tiny meteorologists - they can sense barometric pressure changes and will often take down their webs before storms hit, then rebuild them when conditions improve, all without checking the weather forecast!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Araneus orbweavers, but the bright green legs and cephalothorax combined with the reddish-brown abdomen make it distinctive. Remember: 'Green machine with a red back' to separate it from the more common Cross Orbweaver (which has a white cross pattern) or Marbled Orbweaver (which has more mottled, marble-like patterns).
compareHints: Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver. While the Barn Orbweaver can have reddish tones, it lacks the distinctive bright green front body that makes the Red-backed so recognizable. The color combination is quite unique in this genus - most other Araneus species stick to more muted earth tones throughout their bodies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance).

Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.
Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
